ce:abstract-sec.ce:simple-para: Styrene-butadiene rubber (SBR) is modified either by changing the degree of cross linkage, or by the partial substitution of acrylonitrile for styrene. Four types of SBR-based latex binders (SBRx), which are used as a mixture with sodium carboxymethyl cellulose, are compared with conventional poly(vinylidene fluoride) (PVdF) binder by applying them to LiCoO2 composite electrodes in high-voltage operations up to 4.5 V vs. Li. The results demonstrate not only better electrode performance of SBRx compared with PVdF binder, but also some differences among SBRx binders. Further, they demonstrate good correlation between electrode performance and electrode analysis data by electrochemical impedance spectroscopy and hard X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy, suggesting better coverage with uniformity and stability on LiCoO2 particles composed of SBRx-based binder and deposition products of decomposed electrolyte than that by PVdF binder. The results reveal a clear dependency on the degree of cross linkage, and SBRlow modified by the low degree of cross linkage shows the best cyclability and rate capability. SBRCN, which is modified by acrylonitrile, shows a high solvent uptake and remarkable electrode performance in terms of rate capability and self-discharge suppression.

ce:section.ce:para: Lithium-ion secondary cells comprise four components: positive and negative electrodes, a separator, and an electrolytic solution. Among these, the electrodes are regarded as key components to store and generate electric power. Practical lithium-ion cells employ powdery composite electrodes composed of an active material, a conductive agent, and a binder. The active material is the most important component to determine the energy density of a specific cell system. However, the remaining two components are also crucial materials to maximize the intrinsic performance of active materials and improve it in some cases, although they are electrochemically inactive. As for a binder, poly(vinylidene fluoride) (PVdF) has been used for both the positive and negative electrodes since the first introduction of lithium-ion batteries owing to its preferable chemical properties and electrochemical stability. However, the coverage to protect active material particle surface and the mechanical strength of resultant composites are insufficient to cope with high-potential operations and large volume change during lithium insertion/extraction, and the adhesion strength of the composite layer onto a current collector is not enough to avoid detachment [1–4]. In addition, N-methyl-2-pyrrolidone (NMP) solvent to dissolve PVdF for electrode slurry preparation is combustible and harmful, thereby motivating us to study water-based binders. Accordingly, we have been intensively studying water-based binders for lithium-, sodium-, and potassium-ion batteries [5–10].

For graphite-based negative electrodes of lithium-ion batteries, substitution of water-based polymer for conventional PVdF is a recent trend to increase the packing capacity by decreasing the binder content, and to reduce the production cost of lithium-ion batteries by eliminating the use of NMP. The typical water-based binder for negative electrodes is a mixture of elastic styrene-butadiene rubber (SBR) latex [11] and sodium carboxymethyl cellulose (CMC) as a thickener for an aqueous slurry [12,13]. Furthermore, we studied several new water-based binders, such as poly(acrylic acid) and sodium polyacrylate [7,8], polysaccharides, and lithium polyglutamate [10]. Consequently, silicon composite electrodes using such binders demonstrated superior electrochemical performance compared to those using PVdF.

For the positive electrodes, PVdF remains a major binder, and a full-scale introduction of an alternative binder has not yet been achieved to the best of our knowledge. Previous studies have reported water-based binders through aqueous slurry process for positive electrodes. Guerfi et al. reported that 3.5 V-class LiFePO4 electrodes using an SBR/CMC binder demonstrated good flexibility, sufficient adhesion onto Al foil, and good electrode performance, such as smaller irreversible capacity and good rate capability [14]. Li et al. applied a CMC binder to high-voltage positive electrodes, beyond 4.3 V, such as Li2MnO3-LiMO2 (M = Mn, Ni, Co) which exhibited better cycle performances than PVdF binder [15]. Wang et al. applied a CMC binder to LiNi0.4Mn1.6O4 electrodes and achieved a high discharge capacity exceeding 140 mAh g−1 and suppressed self-discharge, suggesting its potential as an alternative binder to PVdF [16].

Our group reported a study of the SBR/CMC binder for LiCoO2 positive electrodes and demonstrated that it yielded a better cycle performance between 4.5 and 3.0 V than PVdF or CMC binders [9]. Based upon the finding, we decided to extend our study towards development of new binders of SBR by modifying the cross-linkage degree or substituting a certain amount of acrylonitrile monomer for styrene monomer to adjust the physicochemical properties of the binder and improve the electrode performance. Accordingly, we developed new water-based binders containing modified SBR, denoted as SBRx, without compromising the original high adhesion strength and flexibility [11,13]. They were also used as a mixture with CMC thickener, similar to the conventional SBR/CMC binder. In this study, we investigate the applicability of mixtures of SBRx latexes and CMC (SBRx/CMC) as binders to high-voltage LiCoO2 positive electrodes up to 4.5 V vs. Li, in comparison with conventional PVdF and a standard SBR (SBRstd) water-based binder, SBRstd/CMC which was used in our previous work [9,17]. Some of the SBRx/CMC binders demonstrated promising binder properties and provided better electrochemical performances of LiCoO2 electrodes than those of PVdF and SBRstd. The mechanism for the improvement is discussed with the results of the following electrode characterizations: electrolyte uptake, optical microscopy, electron microscopy observation, and hard X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy.

Four types of SBR latexes were prepared and used in this study. The first one was our standard and conventional SBR [9,17], denoted as SBRstd (NIPPON A & L INC.). The second and third ones, denoted as SBRhigh, SBRlow, have different degrees of cross linkage: SBRhigh with a higher degree of cross linkage than SBRstd, and SBRlow with a lower degree of cross linkage than SBRstd, both synthesized by tuning the content of chain transfer agent. The chain transfer agent generally suppresses generation of the cross linkage and increasing the content decreases the cross-linkage degree of SBR. The fourth one is modified by partial substitution of acrylonitrile monomer for styrene, which is denoted as SBRCN. SBRhigh, SBRlow, and SBRCN were synthesized by NIPPON A & L INC. The relation of the cross-linkage degree was estimated from the residual mass ratio of the SBR films (Table 1 ) when the films were immersed in toluene at room temperature for 48 h and dried at 100 °C for 1 h under ambient pressure. The glass transition temperatures, T g, of four different SBR latexes were adjusted to −15 °C to control them to be similarly flexible, as listed in Table 1. T g of SBR is mainly controlled by turning the ratio of monomers, i.e. styrene and butadiene. High styrene/butadiene ratio generally results in high T g of SBR.

Commercially available LiCoO2 (LCO) powder was used as the positive electrode material. Acetylene black (AB, Denka Black Li-400, Denka Co. Ltd.) was used as a conductive agent. Five types of binder materials were used in this study: PVdF (Polysciences, Inc.) as a reference dissolved in NMP, and four types of mixtures comprising CMC (CMC#2200, Daicel FineChem Ltd., substitution degree of 0.8–1.2) and a different SBRx latex (NIPPON A & L, INC.), as shown in Table 1. NMP for PVdF and deionized water for latex binders were used as dispersion agents. LCO, AB, and PVdF were mixed at a ratio of 80:10:10 (m/m) with NMP. LCO, AB, SBRx, and CMC were thoroughly mixed at a ratio of 80:10:0.5:1.5 (m/m) with distilled water. The prepared slurry was coated onto an aluminum foil as a current collector followed by drying at 80 °C under vacuum. To evaluate the electrochemical property of the binders, electrodes without LCO comprising AB:PVdF = 80:20 or AB:SBRx:CMC = 80:5:15 (m/m) were prepared on an aluminum current collector [17].

R2032 coin-type Li cells were assembled in an Ar-filled glove box with an LCO electrode of which the size was 10 mm in diameter, prepared as mentioned previously [17]. Lithium metal foil was used as a counter electrode with a polyolefin separator between them, and a 1.0 mol dm−3 LiPF6 aprotic electrolyte solution comprising ethylene carbonate (EC) and dimethyl carbonate (DMC) at a volume ratio of 1:1 (Kishida Chemical Co., Ltd.) was used. Galvanostatic delithiation–lithiation tests of the LCO electrodes were performed at a current density of 20 mA g−1, corresponding to a C/8 rate for LCO in the voltage ranges of 3.0–4.5 V at approximately 25 °C. The mass loading of LCO ranged from 4.5 to 5.2 mg cm−2.

Electrochemical ac impedance spectroscopy was performed for LCO electrodes after they were discharged to 3.9 V, approximately 50% of the state of charge, in a three-electrode cell to ensure accurate measurements of potential and impedance, with counter and reference electrodes of lithium metal in the frequency range from 100 kHz to 10 mHz at an amplitude of 10 mV.

The electrolyte uptake of the binder was estimated as a swelling index of the binder and composite electrode by measuring the mass increase during the immersion of binder films, approximately 0.3 mm thick, into an EC/DMC solvent, as follows [17]:
1)
prepare a binder liquid with solvent of water or NMP only for PVdF, spread it onto a glass plate, and dry the binder film at 80 °C in a vacuum.
2)
immerse the film in a 1:1 (v/v) mixture of EC/DMC for 24 h.
3)
compare the masses of the film between before (wo) and after immersion (w1). The mass increment corresponds to the solvent uptake:
(1) solvent uptake (%) = [(w1-wo)/ wo] x 100
4)
the film was dried again at 80 °C in a vacuum to remove EC/DMC. The resulting mass (w2) was used to calculate the solubility of the binder:
(2) solubility (%) = [(wo-w2)/ wo] x 100

The electrode surface morphology was observed using an electron microscope (JCM-6000, JEOL, Ltd.). The adhesive strength of the prepared electrodes was measured using a peel tester (STA-1150, A&D Co., Ltd.) and double-sided tape (Scotch tape, SPS-12, 3 M Japan, Ltd.) as described in our previous study [18]. The measurement conditions were as follows: peeling angle of 90°, peeling speed of 10 mm min−1, and load range of 50 N.

Hard X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (HAXPES) spectra were collected using a VG-SCIENTA photoelectron energy analyzer, R-4000 at BL46XU in SPring-8, Japan. Electrochemically tested electrodes were carefully removed from cycled coin cells, rinsed with DMC solvent, dried at room temperature in an Ar-filled glove box, and transferred to the instrument using a transfer vessel without air exposure. The detailed setup and condition of the HAXPES measurement are described in our previous paper [6].

First, we characterized the newly prepared SBRx films before we adapted them as a binder for the LCO electrodes in high-voltage operations. The affinity between the SBRx films and electrolyte solution was examined by measuring the solubility and solvent uptake. The results are summarized in Table 2 , which includes those of PVdF and CMC for comparison. The solubility was negligibly small for all SBRx samples. Therefore, all SBRx were insoluble in the electrolyte solution of the lithium-ion batteries. The overall trend of affinity among the SBRx films was summarized from the results as follows:
1)
A high degree of cross linkage suppresses solvent uptake, while a low degree encourages it.
2)
The introduction of polar functional group –CN, as confirmed by FT-IR (see Fig. S1), enhances solvent uptake.

A large solvent uptake is one of favorable properties for good wettability of the electrode with electrolyte to obtain good accessibility of Li+ ion as well as rate capability of LCO, which will be evaluated through cell tests in the next section. However, the solubility and affinity might differ slightly from those occurring in real electrolyte solutions, as the solvent used for the test does not contain LiPF6.

The affinity between the binder and electrode materials, such as active materials and conductive carbon, is crucial to provide a uniform dispersion of slurries, resulting in a uniform distribution in entire composite electrode. Distribution of LCO, AB, and binder in slurries was observed using an optical microscope. For this observation, all slurries used for electrode preparation were diluted five times by volume with the corresponding solvent, NMP or deionized water, followed by sandwiching them between slide glass and cover glass plates [17]. The PVdF slurry contains agglomerated particles, while the SBRx/CMC ones show uniformly dispersed particles without such an agglomeration (see Fig. S2). This difference is expected to affect the resultant electrode condition and performance.

It should be noted that a simplified notation, SBRx binder, is adopted hereinafter for the mixed binder of SBRx and CMC, as all of the SBRx latexes were used by combining with CMC as binders in this study. Therefore, SBRx electrode means an LCO composite electrode with the mixed binder of SBRx and CMC. Meanwhile, PVdF electrode denotes an LCO electrode with a PVdF binder.

The adhesive strength between a current collector and the composite layer containing a binder, etc. was examined by a 90° peel test with an adhesive tape (see Fig. S3a) [18]. The results are summarized in Table 3 . The composite layer of the PVdF electrode was completely peeled from the Al current collector, and the average load for peeling was 0.06 N cm−1. Furthermore, the values of approximately 0.3 N cm−1 for the SBRx electrodes are much larger than that for PVdF, even though the 3% binder content of them is significantly less than 10% of the PVdF electrode. Clearly, the SBRx binders show a much higher adhesive strength compared with PVdF. No significant difference is exhibited among the adhesive strengths of the SBRx electrodes (see Fig. S3b).

ce:section.ce:section-title: Electrochemical performance of LCO electrodes containing SBRx binders
ce:section.ce:para: The voltage curves of galvanostatic charge and discharge of the LCO electrodes using five types of binders, including conventional PVdF and SBRstd for comparison, are shown in Fig. 1 . Upper voltage limit was set to 4.5 V to observe the binder effect on cycle stability of high voltage operation. All SBRx electrodes delivered a reversible capacity of 175 mAh g−1 at the first cycle, followed by a stable cyclability up to the 50th cycle. However, the PVdF electrode exhibited a growing polarization and fading capacities. This result is most likely consistent with the difference between PVdF and SBRx binders in adhesive strength shown in Table 3, and dispersibility shown in Fig. S2. Fig. 2 shows the variation in discharge capacities and the Coulombic efficiencies of the test results already shown in Fig. 1, which is also summarized in Table 4 . As shown in Fig. 2a, the discharge capacity for the PVdF electrode decreased significantly for 50 cycles to 125 mAh g−1, 71% of the initial capacity, while the SBRx electrodes maintained over 150 mAh g−1, more than 86% of the initial value. Among the SBRx electrodes, the SBRstd and SBRlow electrodes retained a capacity as high as 164 mAh g−1, 93% of the initial value at the 50th cycle. The improved cycle stability of the SBRx electrodes is believed to be due to the uniform dispersion of the electrode materials in the slurry and the tight adhesion of the coated composite layer on electrode substrate as shown above.

In Fig. 2b, the first cycle Coulombic efficiencies for the PVdF electrode exceeds 90%, while those for the SBRx are lower than 90%. This result is due to the irreversible oxidation of CC bonds in the polymerized butadiene unit of the main chain of SBR above 4.2 V vs. Li+/Li, as we have reported previously [9,17] (see Fig. S4, which shows the anodic oxidation of CC bonds of SBRx during early cycles by using 80% AB and 20% binder electrodes). However, the Coulombic efficiencies for the SBRx electrodes increased after the second cycle, and revealed higher average values, exceeding 99%, compared with the PVdF electrode during the 50 cycles, as shown in Table 4. This difference is regarded as being due to the uniformity of the binder coverage on the surface of active material particles as discussed below.

The electrode surface morphology after 50 cycles of the PVdF electrode and SBRX electrodes was observed by SEM. The PVdF electrode shows a roughened surface with severe cracks, and the SBRhigh electrode also shows a harsh surface, presumably reflecting the brittle tendency of SBRhigh binder due to the high degree of cross linkage. However, the SBRstd, SBRlow, and SBRCN electrodes show a smooth surface without cracks (see Fig. S5). This observation is consistent with the difference in capacity retention shown in Fig. 2a.

Fig. 3 compares the rate capability of the five LCO electrodes. The PVdF electrode shows discharge capacities of 175 mAh g−1 at 20 mA g−1 and 88 mAh g−1 at 640 mA g−1, while the SBRx electrodes show better rate capabilities: 175 mAh g−1 at 20 mA g−1 and over 120 mAh g−1 at 640 mA g−1. The SBRCN and SBRlow electrodes, in particular, present over 150 mAh g−1 at 640 mA g−1, which is much higher than the 120 mAh g−1 of the SBRstd electrode. This result shows the similar tendency to the order of solvent uptake shown in Table 2, suggesting that the good affinity of electrodes with electrolyte solution supports the effective supply of lithium ions in the entire composite electrodes for a high rate discharge.

Fig. 4 shows the self-discharge (self-lithiation) test results for the fully charged electrodes using different binders. If the binder and surface deposition effectively passivate the surface of the electrode particles, then self-discharge will be suppressed [17]. Hence, the self-discharge measurement will provide useful information for understanding the effect of coverage on the LCO particles. The electrodes were fully charged to 4.5 V at the 6th cycle; subsequently, the LCO/lithium cells were stored under an open-circuit state for 7 d at room temperature followed by the 6th discharging, and the cycle test was restarted to be continued from the 7th cycle. As shown in Fig. 4 and Table 5 , all the SBRx electrodes maintained higher Coulombic efficiencies after a 7 d storage in a fully charged state compared with the PVdF electrode, indicating suppressed side reactions during the exposure of LCO to a high potential. It is observed that the SBRCN electrode delivers the highest Coulombic efficiency of 92% among all electrodes. This improvement is attributed to the better passivation of the LCO electrode with the SBRCN binder, which is consistent with the results of previous studies [9,17].

Fig. 5 shows the Nyquist plots of the LCO electrodes with different binders after the 1st and 50th cycles. As previously reported for the LCO electrode with PVdF binder [19], the two semicircles are observed at 0.1–100 kHz and 0.1–100 Hz, which are attributed to the resistance of lithium diffusion in the surface film, R f, and that of charge transfer at the surface film/Li x CoO2 particle interface, R ct, respectively, according to the literature [19]. Table 6 presents the estimated values of the resistances by fitting with a simple equivalent circuit shown in Fig. S6. After the 1st cycle, all the SBRx electrodes show similar resistances: R f of ~2 Ω and R ct semicircle from 36 to 37 Ω. However, the PVdF electrode shows lower resistances than those of the SBRx electrodes, which is speculated to be due to the poor coverage of PVdF on the LCO particles. After 50 cycles, the R ct of all the electrodes increased. Particularly, that of the PVdF electrode increased by a factor of more than two, which is consistent with the poor cyclability in Fig. 1 and the roughened surface. This result seems to suggest the sedimentation of decomposition products of electrolyte solution on the electrode surface. Among the SBRx electrodes, the SBRlow electrode shows the lowest R ct after 50 cycles, proving the low resistance of the surface layer formed during 50 cycles, which is consistent with the best cyclability in Fig. 2a and rate capability in Fig. 3 . The SBRCN electrode shows an R f value as large as 50 Ω after 50 cycles, suggesting that the suppressed self-discharge shown in Fig. 4 is probably due to the thicker surface layer preventing self-lithiation.

The difference among SBRx binders in the coverage condition with the binder and surface layer deposited during cycling is suggested in the foregoing results from Figs. 3–5. Therefore, we further evaluated the surface coverage of the electrodes through a direct surface analysis of the electrodes with HAXPES, which was conducted on the LCO electrodes with PVdF and SBRx binders after 10 and 50 charge/discharge cycles. HAXPES measurements using a high excitation energy X-ray of 7938.9 eV can provide information of chemical bonds from the inner and deeper regions to several tens nm of samples [20,21].

It is typical to rinse a sample electrode with DMC before XPS measurements to remove excessive electrolyte salts which might adhere to the electrode and deposit during drying. However, this procedure might rinse away the effective deposited layer to improve the electrode performance. Therefore, we compared the HAXPES spectra of electrodes unrinsed and rinsed with DMC solvent. Figs. 6 and 7
present comparisons of the HAXPES spectra of LCO electrodes with different binders between those unrinsed and rinsed in DMC for a few times. Fig. 6a and b shows the Co 2p HAXPES spectra of LCO electrodes after 10 cycles, unrinsed and rinsed, respectively. Both figures present two clear signals: at ~780 eV assigned to Co 2p3/2, and ~795 eV assigned to Co 2p1/2 [22]. No significant difference was observed between Fig. 6a and b, although the two signals became clear after rinse except for the rinsed SBRCN electrode. For the samples after 50 cycles, Fig. 6c and d also show insignificant difference regardless of the rinse with DMC except for the rinsed PVdF electrode, which is similar to Fig. 6a and b. In the exceptional cases of the rinsed PVdF and SBRCN electrodes, the weak intensities would originate from the differential charging effect related to heterogeneously charged components having poor electrical connections and/or covered by insulating species [23–25]. The results might suggest that the deposited or covering layer accumulated during cycles on the PVdF and SBRCN electrodes are thick insulator and/or heterogeneously soluble in pure DMC during the rinsing process.

Fig. 7a and b shows the O 1s HAXPES spectra of the LCO electrodes after 10 cycles, unrinsed and rinsed, respectively. Both figures present two clear signals at ~529.6 eV assigned to the lattice oxygen of LCO and at 532–535 eV. The later broad signal is known to be deconvoluted to the peaks at ~532.0 eV can be attributed to the oxygen atoms in Li2CO3 and oxygen atoms doubly bound to carbon atoms [26], at ~533.5 eV can be attributed to oxygen atoms singly bound to carbon as in lithium alkyl carbonates ROCO2Li [27], OP(OR)3 [28], and polycarbonate-type compounds [28], and at ~534.6 eV can be assigned to Li x PF y O z formed by the anodic decomposition of LiPF6 with the solvent [22,29]. The comparison between Fig. 7a and b shows an apparent decrease in signal intensities for these decomposition products against those for lattice oxygen after rinse, which proves that the products are removed or dissolved during rinsing. Fig. 7c and d shows the O 1s HAXPES spectra of the LCO electrodes after 50 cycles, and the results exhibit the similar tendency shown in Fig. 7a and b, although the signals for the decomposition products remain explicit even after rinsing, as shown in Fig. 7d, suggesting a thicker deposition layer or the deposition of insoluble products. Some electrodes show broad signals in the extraordinary high energy region of 535–540 eV due to the differential charging effect, indicating heterogeneously charged components having poor electrical connections and/or covered by insulating species. The unwashed electrodes seem to show relatively homogeneous charging compared to the washed ones. Particularly, the SBRCN electrode shows obvious differential charging effects more often than those for the other electrodes, which implies a thick coverage and/or insoluble species heterogeneously distributed on the LCO particles, as discussed on Fig. 6 above.

Fig. 8 shows the C 1s, P 1s, and F 1s HAXPES spectra for the LCO electrodes cycled for 50 cycles and unrinsed and rinsed with DMC. In Fig. 8a and b for the C1s spectra of the unrinsed and rinsed electrodes, respectively, a sharp peak with a relatively high intensity located at ~284.6 eV can be attributed to sp2 type C–C bonding and is mainly observed except for the rinsed LCO electrode with PVdF binder in Fig. 8b. The peak at ~285.0 eV can be attributed to hydrocarbons and is mainly observed in the rinsed PVdF electrode. Two peaks at ~286.2 and ~290.8 eV attributed to C–H and C–F bonds in PVdF [28] are observed for the unrinsed PVdF electrode in Fig. 8a unlike that in the rinsed one in Fig. 8b, indicating the differential charging effect in the rinsed PVdF electrode as confirmed on the O 1s spectrum in Fig. 7d. In addition to the PVdF components, the peak located at ~286.2 eV can be attributed to carbon atoms singly bounded to oxygen (C–O) and the peaks near 290.8 eV are related to CO3 group in ROCO2Li (~290.1 eV) [27] or Li2CO3 (~290.3 eV) [30]. Signal intensities of these peaks related to the decomposition products are relatively low compared to those for sp2 carbon in acetylene black. Only the rinsed PVdF and SBRstd electrodes in Fig. 8b show the peak at ~289.0 eV, which might be attributed to carbon atoms bound to two oxygen atoms as in the carboxylic group (O–CO) [22]. However, the both electrodes have obvious differential charging effects found in the O1s (Fig. 7d), P 1s (Fig. 8d), and F 1s (Fig. 8f) spectra as asymmetric broad peaks at abnormally high energy region. In Fig. 8c and d, the P 1s spectra exhibit a signal at ~2152 eV assigned to LiPF6 [31] and a signal at 2149.7 eV attributed to Li x PF y O z [32] in the PVdF and SBRx electrodes. The two peaks are more distinguishable after the rinsing process of the SBRx electrodes, and the LiPF6 degradation intermediate of Li x PF y O z is detected for the SBRx electrodes as also seen in the F 1s spectra. In Fig. 8e and f of the F 1s spectra, a peak at ~688 eV can be attributed to fluorine atoms in PVdF or in LiPF6 and the intermediate-energy component at~686.6 eV can be related to LiPF6 degradation intermediates such as Li x PF y O z [28]. As Lu et al. reported, this peak may include a contribution from LiPF6 degradation products generated by X-ray exposure during the XPS measurements [22]. In addition, a peak located at ~685 eV assigned to LiF [28] is observed slightly but certainly for the PVdF electrode, while the peaks for the SBRx electrodes are unclear. Because LiF is formed through the reaction between F− released by the decomposition of LiPF6 and Li+, this result suggests that the LCO in the SBRx electrodes is covered and protected more effectively with the binder and deposited product than in the PVdF electrode. We believe that the electrolyte containing LiPF6 salt is absorbed into the binder layer on electrode surface, as suggested by the high solvent uptake in Table 2, and that the decomposition product of the salt also serves as a protective layer for the LCO particles and supports the excellent cyclability, rate capability, and self-discharge suppression. To sum up the HAXPES data from Figs. 6–8, all data are consistent with the preceding results on the binders and their electrodes, which suggest a uniform, stable and preferable coverage on the LCO particles by SBRx (x = std, low, and high) binders rather than by PVdF binder [9]. SBRCN binder produces a thick passivation layer on the LCO particles, but further improvement is required for the coverage homogeneity and increasing surface resistance.

Thus far, we have compared SBRx binders with conventional PVdF binder using LCO electrodes in high-voltage operations up to 4.5 V vs. Li as lithium cell electrodes. The results indicated some of important differences not only between PVdF and SBRx binders, but also among SBRx binders. SBRx binders demonstrated superior electrode performance in terms of adhesion strength, cyclability, rate capability, and self-discharge suppression compared with PVdF binder. Among the SBRx binders, SBRlow demonstrated the optimum performance in terms of cyclability and rate capability. We found that correlation between electrode performances, such as cyclability and self-discharge suppression, and electrode analysis data by electrochemical impedance spectroscopy and HAXPES could be understood in terms of coverage on LCO particles. It was observed that SBRlow and SBRCN with high solvent uptake exhibited remarkable electrode performance in terms of cyclability, rate capability, and self-discharge suppression, as demonstrated above.

Moreover, the comparison of all the data from Figs. 1–5 and Tables 2–6 demonstrated a clear dependence of the binder and electrode properties on the cross-linkage degree, in the order of SBRlow < SBRstd < SBRhigh or SBRlow > SBRstd > SBRhigh. A similar dependency on cross-linkage degree has been reported in our previous study on polyacrylates for Si/graphite electrodes of lithium-ion cells, which suggested a difference in polymer conformation by the cross-linkage [33]. The optimum cross-linkage degree should exist for SBR latex binders as well [33]. The remarkable results of SBRCN are likely due to the strong electron-attracting nature of the –CN functional group interacting with lithium ions, as suggested in previous studies [34,35]. The substitution effect of acrylonitrile on butadiene is yet to be studied specifically. Therefore, we will perform a parameter study on the optimization of cross-linked SBR latex and its –CN substitution in the future.

The high-voltage operation of LCO affords an increase in its capacity and energy density; however, it accompanies the gradual decomposition of electrolyte on the surface of LCO particles. Coating LCO with fine particles of ZrO2, Al2O3, SiO2, etc., which is effective in suppressing electrolyte decomposition, has been intensively studied and proven to be effective for high-voltage operations up to 4.5 V [36]. Although it is a proven excellent technology, it requires additional processes and cost compared with conventional lithium-ion cell material processes. Our idea for the high-voltage operation of LCO in this study is to merely change the binder material without significant change of the conventional production process. Therefore, we are convinced that our idea is more practical than oxide coating, although there are many things to be addressed before the idea can be implemented in real production. Meanwhile, the mechanism for the enhanced performances is not yet elucidated completely. Therefore, we will continue studying SBRx binders by applying them to other high-voltage active materials, such as LiNi0.5Mn1.5O4, or by modifying SBR with functional groups other than the –CN group.
